records.name: Analytical versus clinical validation
records.tldr: Analytical validity concerns whether a test measures reliably. Clinical validity concerns what its result means for a condition or outcome. Clinical utility concerns using that information for a decision.
records.summary: Analytical validity, clinical validity and clinical utility address different questions for a specified assay, specimen, population and intended use. MedlinePlus Genetics distinguishes detection of a genetic variant, its relationship to disease presence or risk, and whether the information helps diagnosis, treatment, management or prevention. Reliable measurement does not by itself establish clinical meaning, and an outcome association does not establish benefit from changing care. For a prediction model, reproducibility of fixed-input output, discrimination, calibrated probabilities and the consequences of model-guided decisions also require distinct evidence. These are related questions rather than a universal sequence that guarantees a useful test.

links.label: FDA: Software as a Medical Device (SaMD)
Wikipedia
MedlinePlus Genetics: analytical validity, clinical validity and utility
Jennings et al.: AMP/CAP somatic sequencing-panel validation recommendations (2017)
FDA: companion diagnostics and specified treatment uses
FDA: understanding unapproved use of approved drugs

notes: Start a claim worksheet with the population and treatment setting, specimen and method version, measured or predicted outcome, time horizon and proposed decision. A molecule measurement, drug ranking in a dish and outcome prediction from earlier patients are different claims. For risk, retain whether the estimate assumes usual care or no treatment; for a drug experiment, retain the drug, dose and combination. Leave unavailable details unknown. Then separate the tested material and quality, biological interpretation and alternatives, prediction, proposed action and evidence of benefit. Mark each measured, inferred, proposed or unknown. A sound measurement does not automatically support the later steps.

Consider a fictional report that calls a protein-rich stored tumour a Drug A responder. Its study related protein abundance to shrinkage among people all receiving Drug A for advanced Cancer X. The measurement and response association can be useful, but there is no untreated or alternative-treatment comparison establishing greater benefit from A. Applying it after surgery also changes the setting. Ask what comparison shows improved outcomes from choosing A with this result in the proposed setting. Confirmation of protein abundance answers whether that signal is real, while postoperative benefit remains a separate question. A favourable prognostic result does not itself justify omitting standard treatment.

An evidence card records population, stage, treatment context and selection; specimen, handling, assay version and quality criteria; the reference condition or care comparator and its limitations; outcome and measurement time; the analysis plan, all tuning and independent evaluation; failed samples, dropout and missing outcomes; and sample size, intervals and remaining uncertainty. A response endpoint is not recurrence or survival. A preclinical card names the actual model and tested claim; an observational clinical association retains possible confounding. Neither alone establishes that the proposed clinical action helps. A headline metric also needs the consequences of false positive and false negative calls attached to the action. Distinguish prespecified analyses from exploratory searches, keep their tuning history, and seek confirmation that does not reuse the search. State whether a treatment-study denominator includes everyone assigned, only those treated or only those evaluable.

For analytical performance, request the detection limit with its target level, input amount, specimen and detection probability; precision within runs and across days, operators, instruments and reagent lots; agreement with an appropriate independent reference; attempted-sample failure rate and reasons; and specimen handling, preservation and interference testing. The 2017 AMP/CAP recommendations concern next-generation sequencing panels for somatic variants. They ask for performance by variant class and relevant reference materials, depth and sample numbers. They describe a lower detection limit at which 95 per cent of samples are reliably detected, but also explain why observing 19 or 20 successes in 20 trials does not by itself establish that reliability with confidence. This is an assay-specific example, not a universal validation protocol. Fresh and delayed specimens can differ, and measurement variation must be understood before interpreting a trend. Self-agreement alone does not establish accuracy.

Put the decision before ordering. Write what positive, negative, uncertain and failed results would change, including proposed treatment omission, confirmation or another sample. Compare existing pathology and other tests, and record the decision deadline, finite tissue, time, travel, uncertainty and financial burden. Name who interprets the result, who owns the clinical recommendation and when further testing is unlikely to help that decision. A result arriving after the decision closes may not serve its intended use. The worksheet exposes assumptions rather than calculating a treatment choice; urgency does not establish validity.

In the fictional postoperative protein-test case, possible next steps are checking the actual companion-diagnostic requirement and whether this assay meets it, inspecting the Drug A evidence, considering a trial of the relevant strategy, or declining a tissue-consuming test that would not change the decision. The exact laboratory, service, version and intended use matter. A research-use label, laboratory certification, development designation or report drug list cannot replace the claim-specific evidence. A companion test is tied to specified treatment use. Clinician-led off-label use, access, payment and suitability are additional questions, not promises made by a molecular report. Fast-track and breakthrough-therapy designations are not marketing approval; accelerated approval is a distinct approval pathway, not just a development designation.

Research can have a defined value without selecting treatment: checking a mechanism, explaining discordant assays or generating a future hypothesis. Name the reviewer and what would count as a useful answer rather than extending an endless chain of tests. Attribute unpublished company data and state which methods and results were available to inspect; unavailable evidence does not prove the claim false. In a fictional high/low recurrence-risk test for which neither answer changes recommended care and no relevant study is open, the immediate value for that treatment decision is limited. A separate research or personal-information goal should be weighed against burden, uncertainty and alternatives. A changed treatment decision is not itself demonstrated benefit and can add unnecessary treatment.

records.name: External validation
records.tldr: External evaluation estimates model performance on data not used to develop or tune it. The patients, setting and methods determine which transportability question it addresses; it does not by itself establish useful clinical decisions.
records.summary: External evaluation applies an existing model to data outside its development and compares predictions with observed outcomes. The TRIPOD-Cluster explanation includes later-period data collected by the same investigators as well as data from another hospital, country or care setting. A different platform is not a universal requirement. Apparent performance uses the development data and can be optimistic. Internal validation with resampling can estimate optimism and performance for new people from the same source population; it is evidence about a different question, rather than no result. External evaluation quantifies performance and its uncertainty instead of conferring a universal pass or fail. Keep the locked method, population, outcome, follow-up and differences from development visible.

links.label: Wikipedia
Debray et al.: TRIPOD-Cluster explanation, development and evaluation (2023)
Michiels et al.: repeated-split reanalysis of seven microarray prognosis studies (2005)

notes: Follow the people behind a performance plot: eligibility, selection, care, sample quality, failures and missing outcomes. Identify every variable-selection, preprocessing and threshold choice and whether outcomes were known when those choices were made. Good performance on ideal specimens or the development patients may not describe practice. External evaluation uses data outside development, which can differ in hospital, calendar period, handling or care. The data and evaluation need to be independent of the tuning decisions; a new company logo supplies no such guarantee.

Two fictional slides illustrate the boundary. Slide A uses Hospital A patients and their known outcomes to select variables and a threshold, then reports performance on those same A patients. That is apparent performance; repeating the computation can check reproducibility without providing a new independent population test. Slide B fixes preprocessing, variables and threshold using A before applying the locked method to separate Hospital B patients. It reports B performance and the failed-test denominator, with no B outcomes fed back into tuning. This supports evaluation outside development, while suitable population, uncertainty, calibration and usefulness of clinical decisions remain separate questions. The patient icons are schematic and neither slide supplies a measured performance value.

Michiels and colleagues reanalysed the seven largest published microarray cancer-prognosis studies in their 2005 report using multiple random training and evaluation sets. They found unstable gene signatures and overoptimistic published estimates; five of the seven did not classify patients better than chance. That historical result supports retaining the entire selection and evaluation process, not a conclusion that every molecular model fails or that this one analysis establishes a universal validation method.

A model evaluated at a second hospital may still address advanced treated disease rather than the proposed postoperative use. Discrimination asks whether outcomes are ranked usefully; calibration asks whether stated probabilities agree with observed frequencies in comparable groups. Good ranking can coexist with inflated risk estimates, and good prognostic probabilities do not establish benefit from a treatment printed beside them. There is no single performance cutoff that makes every decision appropriate. If unchanged Hospital A samples are rerun, request an evaluation set held out from every tuning choice, a locked method, target population and outcome, all failure denominators and uncertainty. Internal resampling and independent external evaluation answer different performance questions; neither name alone is a clinical-use verdict.

records.name: Positive predictive value (PPV)
records.tldr: Positive predictive value is the fraction of positive results that match the reference condition rather than being false positive calls. It depends on prevalence and the test's actual performance.
records.summary: Positive predictive value is the proportion of positive test calls that meet a specified reference condition: true positives divided by true plus false positives. A positive result can be a true positive or a false positive; a false positive is a positive call in someone without that reference condition. Negative predictive value uses negative calls as its denominator. These differ from sensitivity and specificity, which start with reference-condition groups. The population base rate, reference standard, threshold and actual assay performance determine how the fractions should be interpreted.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA: statistical guidance for reporting diagnostic-test studies

notes: Separate the index-test result from a defined reference condition. Sensitivity is TP/(TP+FN), the positive fraction among reference cases; specificity is TN/(TN+FP), the negative fraction among reference non-cases. PPV is TP/(TP+FP), the reference-case fraction among positive calls; NPV is TN/(TN+FN), the reference-noncase fraction among negative calls. Base rate means prevalence of that reference condition in the intended tested population. Regrouping the same people by positive calls changes a denominator without adding participants.

Fictional groups each contain 1,000 people, with complete reference assessment, no indeterminate results and assumed sensitivity 80 per cent and specificity 90 per cent. At 10 per cent prevalence there are TP 80, FN 20, FP 90 and TN 810: PPV is 80/170, about 47.1 per cent, and NPV 810/830, about 97.6 per cent. At 50 per cent prevalence the counts are 400, 100, 50 and 450: PPV is 88.9 and NPV 81.8 per cent. At 5 per cent prevalence there are 40 true and 95 false positive calls, giving PPV 29.6 per cent. The examples hold performance fixed to isolate base rate; real populations can change performance too. High NPV can coexist with missed cases and is not a universal absence-of-disease guarantee.

Use test results and suitable independent reference outcomes in the intended population. Keep the locked threshold, condition definition, assay version, all four counts, confidence intervals and handling of missing or indeterminate results. Verifying only positive calls, using an imperfect comparator or borrowing another population's prevalence can mislead. Without a reference that establishes the condition, positive and negative percent agreement may be the appropriate descriptions; agreement does not prove either method correct. Imaging and pathological response are different assessments, so a comparison needs the population, regimen, definition, timing and surgical reference. Accuracy alone establishes neither treatment benefit nor safe surgery omission, and population fractions are not automatic personal probabilities.

Fictional examples hold sensitivity at 90 per cent and specificity at 95 per cent to isolate the base rate, with complete reference assessment and no indeterminate tests. Among 1,000 people with condition prevalence 10 per cent, 100 have the condition: 90 test positive, while 45 of the 900 without it test positive. PPV is 90/(90 + 45), about 67 per cent. At 2 per cent prevalence, 20 have the condition: 18 test positive and 49 of the other 980 test positive. PPV is 18/(18 + 49), about 27 per cent. The same assumed sensitivity and specificity therefore yield very different positive-call fractions. Actual performance can also change across populations. A negative test retains its detection limits, specimen timing and pretest context rather than guaranteeing absence of disease.

records.name: Targeted therapy
records.tldr: A targeted treatment acts on a specified molecule or process. Some block a cancer dependence; others use a molecule as an address for delivery or immune recruitment. The target name alone does not establish benefit or normal-tissue safety.
records.summary:
Targeted treatments include small molecules and therapeutic antibodies with different actions. A molecule whose function supports cancer growth and a surface molecule used to deliver an active drug or recruit an immune cell have different roles. Detecting either does not by itself establish that the finished treatment reaches its target, changes a relevant function or helps in a particular clinical setting.

Some treatments require a specified biomarker test; others have no target-expression selection test in the relevant label. Keep the actual drug, disease, treatment setting and testing rule together. NCI describes resistance and potentially serious adverse effects of targeted therapy. Neither relative normal-tissue sparing, mild toxicity nor a permanent response follows from the word targeted.

links.label: Wikipedia
NCI: targeted therapy, different antibody actions, resistance and adverse effects
TRODELVY U.S. label: indications, mechanism and named pharmacokinetic measurements
KIMMTRAK U.S. label: gp100 peptide-HLA-A*02:01/CD3 recognition and indication

FDA: Considerations for the Development of CAR T Cell Products (January 2024)
FDA: Oncology Therapeutic Radiopharmaceuticals, Nonclinical Studies and Labeling (August 2019)
Mertins et al.: separate RNA, protein and phosphoprotein layers (2016)
FDA: Investigational New Drug application overview
FDA: Biologics License Applications for CBER-regulated products

notes: Target, mechanism and evidence. A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on, and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect; a target name does not show that the target is reachable, required by the cancer, or that changing it does useful work. Binding to a purified protein, engagement in the relevant cell (the cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding in cells and tissues), a measured effect with controls, and benefit and harm in a stated clinical setting each need their own evidence, and a blood concentration is not the concentration at an intracellular target. In-cell thermal profiling can pick up indirect as well as direct targets (Ball et al. 2020). If an antibody is shown to bind a protein on cancer cells and growth is unchanged, binding is supported; dependence on the protein, inhibition of its function, delivery by a finished payload-bearing product, safety and benefit are not. A molecule used as an address for delivery and a molecule whose function the cell depends on are different roles.

What NCI says about the class. Targeted therapy was once expected to be less toxic than chemotherapy but can cause serious side effects, cancer cells can become resistant to it, and it may work best combined with other targeted therapy or with treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation (NCI page, HTML read).

A product proposal identifies the clinical problem, disease setting, treatment intent, alternatives and measurable goal; the exact target, specimen and method; accessible protein or peptide-HLA presentation and normal-tissue evidence with sampling limits; and the complete binder, linker, payload or cell design and mechanism. It records the relevant human comparison or explicitly limited preclinical evidence, product-specific safety monitoring, management capability and stopping rules. Keep manufacture, quality release, sponsor, site and access pathway separate from benefit. Reviewing existing data, consuming tissue for an experiment, manufacturing and administering treatment are different commitments with their own rationale and responsible owner. A target shortlist or recipe analogy establishes none of their benefit or safety.

Questions follow the product. For a cytotoxic antibody-drug conjugate, assess antibody, linker and payload together, delivery and exposure, tested resistance steps and the design-specific role of internalisation; FDA's March 2024 clinical-pharmacology guidance has this scope. For an engager or cell product, ask about cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity and other neurologic effects, healthy-tissue recognition, tissue access and what can persist after dosing stops. FDA's January 2024 CAR T-cell guidance describes product-specific recognition, expansion, persistence and toxicity management; it does not supply incidence for every engager. For a radioligand, ask how the imaging relates to that therapeutic product's distribution, organ absorbed doses and organ limits. FDA's August 2019 document addresses nonclinical studies and labeling, not a universal clinical dose threshold. Tracer uptake supplies no CAR-T safety threshold. For a T-cell-receptor proposal, ask which peptide-HLA target is recognised and how specificity, natural presentation and function were tested; receptor sequences or expanded clones alone leave these questions open.

Product Q is a fictional investigational conjugate against surface protein M, with a specified antibody, cleavable linker and cell-damaging payload. Adults with progressing metastatic solid cancer after prior treatment are the setting, and the immediate proposal is to review existing data before designing a laboratory experiment. No manufacture, treatment or new sample collection is proposed. The dossier has M RNA measurements from one tumour biopsy and Q activity in target-bearing cultured cells, without direct surface measurement, relevant healthy-tissue tests or a human comparison. Supplier participation, access and site arrangements are unknown. These findings support a research hypothesis about Q, not demonstrated clinical benefit or evidence borrowed from another M-targeted format.

Complete the fictional Q card by retaining accessible tumour protein, healthy-tissue effects, full-product delivery and relevant human outcomes as missing evidence. A research lead first reviews methods, controls and Q-specific product data; this existing-data review consumes no tissue. Pause experiment planning if product identity or usable evidence remains unavailable, and ask which Q-specific result would change the experiment plan. RNA abundance is a different observation from accessible surface protein. Mertins and colleagues measured RNA, protein and phosphoprotein layers in primary breast cancers; that work is not a cell-surface-accessibility or treatment-selection assay. Confirming protein would answer another premise while leaving benefit unproven.

Now change only the fictional request: after complete tumour removal, someone proposes manufacturing Q and administering it to prevent recurrence because M RNA was abundant, an IND is said to be active and a supplier offers manufacture. The setting and commitments have changed, while the dossier is still one biopsy RNA signal plus cultured-cell activity. Neither that evidence nor the attributed investigational milestone or supply offer establishes postoperative benefit. Ask the clinical team for Q-specific human evidence or a relevant protocol, the sponsor which product and protocol are covered, and the readiness owner about delivery requirements. In the United States an effective Investigational New Drug application is not marketing approval, and submission of a Biologics License Application is not its approval. A manufacturing quote cannot confirm supply, consent, review, delivery and monitoring as a whole. With only this dossier, evidence and pathway review are justified; manufacture or administration is not justified by the supplied information. Speculative availability does not promise access or protection against recurrence.

records.name: Train, validation and test split discipline
records.tldr: Training data fit a model, validation data guide choices, and reserved evaluation data test the locked version. The split must match the intended population and prediction task. Choices made using evaluation results make those data part of model development.
records.summary: Training data fit a model, validation data guide choices, and final evaluation data test the locked version. The split needs to match the intended claim; no single split proportion establishes validity. The TRIPOD+AI guidance defines evaluation data as data used to estimate model performance that are distinct from the data used to train the model, tune hyperparameters or select a model, with no overlap in participants (Collins and colleagues, 2024). It asks authors to describe the target population and intended purpose, and to define the outcome and its time horizon. Many cells or repeated wells from one donor are not many independent donors, so a new-donor test has to reserve whole donors across every fitting and tuning choice. Different holdouts answer different questions. In a 2025 benchmark, models were fitted on single perturbations plus 62 of 124 double perturbations and scored on the other 62 double perturbations, repeated over five random partitions, and the same study separately tested prediction of unseen single perturbations in CRISPR interference datasets (Ahlmann-Eltze and colleagues, 2025). Simple baselines, a no-change model and an additive model, were part of the comparison.

links.label: Wikipedia
Collins et al., TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods (BMJ 2024)
Ahlmann-Eltze et al., Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines (Nature Methods 2025)

notes: Evaluation card in words (a reading guide). Input and cost: the data, their provenance and the independent units; computation adds no tissue, but generating reference assays or outcomes has its own cost. Output and units: a named error or discrimination metric, calibration where relevant, uncertainty, and subgroup and failure denominators. Rule and threshold: the version, preprocessing and decision cutoff fixed before final evaluation, with no universal passing cutoff. Failure modes: leakage, overlap, a mismatched outcome, selective missing data or a changed population. Validation tier: task-specific performance evidence, with regulatory status and helpful clinical use as separate questions.

Fictional worked example. A dataset holds cells from 20 donors, and each donor's cells are split between training and testing. Every one of the 20 donors was seen during fitting, so the result addresses a within-donor question and cannot establish performance on new donors; for that question whole donors must be reserved across fitting and tuning (for illustration 16 donors for development and 4 reserved, 16 + 4 = 20, with no recommended proportion).

Fictional worked example. Withholding more cells exposed to intervention X does not show that the response to intervention Y can be predicted. For an unseen-intervention claim, Y's measured response must be absent from fitting and tuning, and the donor, batch and intervention relationships must be kept visible.

Figure reading (fictional identities, light and dark renders agree): panel 1 keeps donors D1 and D2 on both sides, with new cells only; panel 2 fits on D1 and D2 and reserves D3 and D4, a new-donor question; panel 3 fits on use of intervention X and reserves the response to Y, which is absent from fitting and tuning. Donor and intervention splits ask different generalisation questions, and no panel claims performance.

records.name: Calibration: reliability diagrams and the Brier score
records.tldr: Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies for the same population, outcome and time horizon. Correct ranking or a correct overall average is insufficient.
records.summary: Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed outcome frequencies in a defined population and time horizon. A model can rank people well while overstating their risks. Calibration curves and suitable summaries assess agreement with uncertainty. The Brier score averages squared differences between predicted probabilities and individual binary outcomes; it assesses overall prediction error rather than calibration alone. Incomplete follow-up and competing events need methods matched to the predicted outcome.

links.label: Wikipedia: Brier score
Graf et al., Assessment and comparison of prognostic classification schemes for survival data (Statistics in Medicine 1999)
Wikipedia
Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics.
Evaluation of clinical prediction models (part 2): how to undertake an external validation study.

notes: Compare predicted and observed frequencies across risk groups or a flexible calibration curve, with finite-sample uncertainty. Calibration-in-the-large compares the average prediction with the overall outcome rate. Under the named calibration model, slope below 1 suggests predictions that are too extreme and above 1 insufficient spread; intercept near 0 and slope near 1 still do not guarantee agreement everywhere on a flexible curve. A constant prediction can match average risk without ranking anyone. Conversely, high discrimination does not establish probability accuracy.

Two fictional 100-person groups have complete five-year outcomes. Predicting 20 and 40 per cent when 10 and 30 events occur preserves their group order but predicts 60 events instead of 40. In a second independent example, predictions of 10 and 50 per cent with 20 and 40 events give 60 predicted and 60 observed overall, or 30 per cent of 200, while both group predictions remain wrong. These invented comparisons illustrate distinct failures; they do not forecast a particular patient's outcome.

Retain predictions stored before outcomes, model and assay versions, endpoint, target population, treatment era and horizon. Compare frequencies at the same time using a calibration curve or named summary and uncertainty. Treating people censored before the horizon as event-free can mislead; account for incomplete follow-up and relevant competing events. Changed eligibility, care or baseline outcome frequency can change calibration, and an updated model needs evaluation. Checking only an overall average or displaying a narrow numerical range establishes little about model or input uncertainty. Calibration neither identifies which individual will have an event nor establishes benefit from acting on the model.

records.name: Laboratory certification and test authorization
records.tldr: Laboratory certification addresses the laboratory and its testing quality. Product authorization and evidence that a particular test use helps patients answer separate questions.
records.summary: The U.S. Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments program sets laboratory-quality requirements for testing human specimens. CMS distinguishes analytical oversight under that program from clinical validity, which concerns what a result means for a clinical condition. A research-use label describes intended purpose; a laboratory-developed-test description concerns how and where a test is developed and used. FDA product authorization concerns a specified product and intended use. These descriptions can coexist and do not form one universal ladder of clinical usefulness or payment.

notes: The CMS FAQ is used here for the analytical-oversight versus clinical-validity distinction, not its historical discussion of FDA authority over laboratory-developed tests. Current procedural history is retained in the separate FDA LDT-rule record.

An entry in FDA establishment registration or device listing does not itself mean that the facility or device is approved, cleared or authorized. Registration and product authorization are separate claims.

records.name: Companion diagnostic
records.tldr: A companion diagnostic provides information required for a corresponding treatment to be used safely and effectively within its specified context. The result is one part of a treatment decision.
records.summary: The category concerns a device and a corresponding treatment use. FDA describes roles involving likely benefit, serious-adverse-effect risk or specified treatment monitoring. Check both the treatment and diagnostic labeling, including specimen, disease, biomarker and decision rule. A molecular report listing a drug is not by itself a companion-diagnostic authorization. Similar gene names do not establish assay interchangeability, and a positive result does not promise a response.

U.S. CLIA control rules require applicable control results to be acceptable before patient results are reported. Whether to repeat a measurement or use another specimen depends on the actual test and laboratory criteria.

records.name: Companion diagnostics
records.tldr: A companion diagnostic supplies information needed for a corresponding medicine to be used safely and effectively. Its labeling defines the intended use of the result.
records.summary: FDA describes companion diagnostics as devices that supply essential information for a corresponding treatment. Their roles can include identifying likely benefit, increased risk of serious adverse effects or a specified monitoring need. The treatment label and diagnostic labeling retain the relevant disease, specimen, biomarker and decision rule. Some devices have documented group labeling for specified oncology therapies. Similar analyte names do not establish assay interchangeability, and a label-matched result does not guarantee individual benefit or complete clinical suitability.

Makes labeling and measurement context checkable

A result alone does not establish individual benefit
Different assays are not interchangeable without supporting evidence

records.name: Intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol analysis
records.tldr: Analysing every patient in the group they were randomised to, whether or not they actually took the treatment. It preserves the fairness of randomisation and reflects what happens when a treatment is prescribed in real life; per-protocol analysis, by contrast, counts only those who complied.
records.summary: ITT is the primary analysis for superiority trials because excluding non-compliers or early dropouts reintroduces bias. Per-protocol analyses matter for non-inferiority trials, where non-compliance can mask a real difference. 'Modified ITT' variants exclude patients who never received a dose or lacked a baseline measurement and should be pre-specified. 'Response-evaluable' populations in single-arm trials inflate response rates by dropping early progressors, and 'safety population' counts patients as treated. Trial and drug pages on this site report ITT results unless stated.

records.name: Lead time, and lead-time bias
aka: lead time in prostate cancer screening
records.tldr: Finding a cancer earlier starts the survival clock sooner, even if the date of death does not change. Counting that extra time as longer life is lead-time bias. Survival measured from diagnosis alone cannot establish that screening saves lives.
records.summary:
Lead time is the interval between the moment a screening test finds a cancer and the moment that cancer would have been diagnosed because it caused symptoms. Lead-time bias is what happens when survival is measured from diagnosis: a man whose cancer is found five years earlier appears to survive five years longer even if the date of his death is unchanged. It is why survival from diagnosis is unreliable on its own as a measure of whether a screening programme works, and why randomised screening trials report mortality in the whole invited population instead.

For prostate-specific antigen screening, estimated lead time depends on the definition and population. The following numbers are model estimates from specified settings, not a ranking of lead times across cancers. Draisma and Etzioni ran three independently built models of prostate cancer progression and detection, all calibrated to Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results incidence in United States men aged 54 to 80 between 1985 and 2000. Among screen-detected cancers that would have surfaced in the man's lifetime, mean lead time was 5.4 to 6.9 years across the three models; the original MISCAN model fitted instead to the Rotterdam section of the European screening trial gave 7.9 years. Published estimates before that work spanned 3 to 12 years. The three models agreed closely with each other for any single definition of lead time and disagreed substantially across definitions, which is the paper's real finding: the number is a property of the question, not of the disease.

The consequence is practical. Lead time is what generates overdiagnosis: if the lead time is longer than the man's remaining life, the cancer would never have troubled him, and the same modelling put overdiagnosis at 23 to 42 percent of screen-detected cancers in the United States calibration and 66 percent in the Rotterdam one. It is also why the 2018 United States task force statement expresses benefit as deaths and metastatic cases prevented per 1,000 men screened over about 13 years rather than as a survival rate, and why the two 2009 randomised trials, ERSPC and PLCO, are the evidence rather than any registry series.

notes: Why a five-year survival rate cannot settle a screening argument. Three biases push it up without anyone living longer: lead-time bias, because the clock starts earlier; length bias, because a test that samples the population at intervals preferentially catches slow-growing cancers that sit around waiting to be found; and overdiagnosis, because cancers that would never have surfaced are added to the numerator of survivors. All three run in the same direction. Mortality in a randomised invited population is immune to all three, which is why it is the endpoint the trials used.

Lead time is not the same as overdiagnosis, although the two are produced by the same mechanism. Lead time is how much earlier the diagnosis came. Overdiagnosis is the case where the lead time exceeded the rest of the man's life, so the diagnosis never needed to come at all. A long lead time with a long life left is exactly what screening is for.

Lead time is the interval between defined earlier and later detection events. Lead-time bias occurs when that timing difference is mistaken for a better outcome. In a fictional course, detection at year 4 and death at year 6 gives two years from diagnosis. Moving detection to year 3 with death still at year 6 gives three recorded years without adding life. Similarly, labelling post-treatment recurrence at a blood signal before imaging confirmation can mechanically lengthen survival measured from recurrence. Align the endpoint, qualifying event and clock origin. Ten months of detection lead time is not ten added months of life. Earlier effective intervention could help, but its benefit needs separate evidence; correcting the clock alone does not solve selection, confounding or missing follow-up.

Length bias favours conditions with longer detectable preclinical periods. Overdiagnosis means detecting disease that would not have caused clinical harm during the person's lifetime. Neither is another name for lead-time bias. Screening examples explain the distinctions but cannot establish their magnitude in post-treatment molecular monitoring.

A monitoring strategy includes its schedule, positive-result rule and resulting action. Comparing that strategy with a meaningful alternative from a common origin, such as randomisation, can assess clinical outcomes and harms. Counting all assigned participants avoids selecting only those with detectable earlier signals. Analysis must also address when groups entered, how follow-up ended, whether positive tests triggered extra imaging and whether people without prior detection were omitted. c-TRAK TN tested a specific blood-surveillance and intervention design; its detection and feasibility findings do not establish a beneficial intervention window for every early signal. A fictional contrast of median survival of 24 months after blood detection versus 18 after imaging detection, without a common-origin comparison, cannot show that testing saves lives. Some or all of the difference could arise from the earlier clock or other group differences.

The same timing distinction extends beyond the prostate-screening context of this record. Historical breast-cancer surveillance trials illustrate why strategy and outcome must stay together. Rosselli Del Turco and colleagues' 1994 trial enrolled 1,243 surgically treated patients with unilateral invasive breast cancer and no metastases. Adding six-monthly chest radiographs and bone scans detected more isolated intrathoracic and bone metastases, 112 versus 71, and the report described earlier detection of recurrences in that group; five-year relapse-free survival, which stops at detection, was significantly lower with intensive follow-up, while five-year mortality was 18.6% versus 19.5%, with no mortality improvement reported. The separate GIVIO trial enrolled 1,320 women and reported no overall-survival or quality-of-life difference, and no significant difference in time to recurrence detection. Thus the trials should not both be described as showing earlier detection: only the first reported it. Their results do not establish equivalence or the effects of modern imaging and treatment, and a nonsignificant comparison is not proof of exactly zero benefit.

In ctDNA monitoring studies, measured lead time is the date of a defined later event minus the date of the first qualifying positive blood sample, and it is conditional: a median over people with both an earlier positive and a later recurrence leaves out recurrences with no earlier positive, and people who are positive but have not yet recurred are censored. In a prospective breast-cancer study with blood taken every 3 months in the first year and every 6 months after, detection preceded clinical relapse by a median of 10.7 months (95% CI 8.1 to 19.1) in a combined cohort of 144, and brain-only relapse was detected in 1 of 6 patients (Garcia-Murillas 2019). Because draws and scans are both intermittent, the gap begins at an observed draw and cannot locate biological onset, and an earlier signal shows earlier detection and not longer survival, which is the lead-time bias problem.

State how lead time was estimated. A simple median of completed positive-to-recurrence intervals is conditional on that selected group; a time-to-event analysis can also incorporate censored follow-up. People without a prior positive and people positive without a later recurrence therefore need explicit dispositions under the study definition. They are not automatically zero-month, infinite or missing intervals interchangeable across studies.

A fictional timing problem illustrates why group entry matters: if a group is defined by a blood-positive result at month 6, its members had to remain observable until that result. Assigning their earlier follow-up to the positive group can create immortal-time bias. A prespecified landmark or a time-varying exposure analysis addresses different timing questions; the comparison must state its origin, eligibility and handling of later events. This is a study-design reading rule, not evidence that a surveillance policy improves outcomes.

records.name: Investigational New Drug application
records.tldr: This application supports a specified investigation or treatment-access use of a drug in the United States. It is separate from permission to market the product.
records.summary: An Investigational New Drug application contains nonclinical, manufacturing and clinical-protocol information for defined investigational use. Becoming effective does not establish that the product benefits a person or is approved for marketing, and a clinical hold can prevent use. A New Drug Application or Biologics License Application instead requests marketing authorization. Submission, acceptance for filing, an application becoming effective and a marketing decision are different events. The applicable route and product version matter.

notes: For an ordinary new IND, FDA describes a 30-calendar-day period after receipt before an investigation may begin, unless FDA gives earlier notification or imposes a hold. Expanded-access INDs and protocols have route-specific rules; no application number establishes a treatment start date.

Product identity matters alongside the proposed use. A redesigned cell product or personalised formulation cannot acquire another product's evidence or authorisation merely by sharing a target, ingredient category or platform name. FDA assesses nonclinical, manufacturing and clinical-protocol information for the proposed investigation. Ask whether the cited data and permission actually cover that product version and plan; a supplier's earlier authorisation is not itself permission for a different use.

records.name: Off-label
records.tldr: Off-label use means using an approved medicine outside its approved labeling. The evidence for that particular use and whether it will be paid for need separate assessment.
records.summary: A different disease, dose or route can make use of an approved medicine off label. FDA states that clinicians generally may prescribe an approved drug for an unapproved use when they consider it medically appropriate, but the original approval does not establish safety and effectiveness for that use. The supporting evidence can vary. A product never approved for any use is investigational rather than simply off label; clinical trials and expanded access have different arrangements. Approval, a guideline recommendation and insurance coverage are not interchangeable decisions.

Product B has never been approved and is in a trial: ask about its protocol, site, cohort and eligibility. Product C is described as single-patient IND access: ask who supplies it, who takes clinical responsibility and what treatment plan and reviews apply. None of those descriptions establishes benefit or selects a treatment. A different dose and unapproved indication for an approved medicine also starts as an off-label question, although a trial can study it.

records.name: CAR-T cell therapy
records.tldr: CAR-T therapy uses T cells carrying an engineered receptor. Approved products treat selected blood cancers, with product-specific eligibility and safety requirements.
records.summary:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

notes: Generation labels describe common signaling architectures. First-generation constructs use an activation domain, often CD3 zeta; second-generation designs add one costimulatory region; third-generation designs combine two. Fourth-generation and later labels vary across authors. More domains do not establish better patient outcomes. The full binder, spacer, anchor, signaling arrangement and cell preparation still matter.

CD28 and 4-1BB are borrowed intracellular signaling regions, not separately administered receptors. Kawalekar compared metabolic and memory features in defined human-cell experiments. Ramos co-infused two specified second- and third-generation products in lymphoma; different expansion and persistence did not isolate comparative clinical benefit. Neither study ranks all products by signaling-domain name.

Binding, surface CAR expression, activation, proliferation and completed target-cell killing are distinct readouts. Compare otherwise matched constructs, target-positive and target-negative cells, healthy-tissue targets and unstimulated activity. Hudecek found that particular IgG-derived spacers could support killing in a dish yet impair activity in mouse models through Fc interactions.

A peptide-HLA target is an exception to blanket HLA-independent descriptions. Rafiq tested a WT1 peptide presented by HLA-A*02:01 in cell and mouse models; this was a proof of concept, not evidence that every intracellular protein or every HLA type is addressable by that construct.

A 2024 preprint used a pooled signaling-domain library, repeated stimulation and single-cell sequencing to study how domain arrangement affected T-cell states over time. Its membrane-proximal-domain findings are construct-and-assay observations, not a clinical ranking of domains or a validation of pooled-screen hits as treatments.

FDA initiated boxed-warning changes in 2024 for the risk of T-cell malignancies after the then-approved BCMA- or CD19-directed autologous CAR T-cell products. Its communication calls for lifelong monitoring for secondary malignancies. This is a scoped regulatory warning, not a claim that every type of engineered immune cell has the same risk.

In June 2025, FDA eliminated REMS requirements for the named autologous CAR T-cell products in its notice. Product warnings and safety monitoring continued. The manufacturer postmarketing observational studies with 15-year follow-up described in that notice are different from the lifelong patient-monitoring statement in the earlier safety communication.

Relapse mechanisms need separate investigation. Sotillo found CD19 sequence and splicing changes affecting recognition in B-ALL relapse material and experiments. Deng found infusion-product transcriptional features associated with outcomes in a selected cohort of 24 large B-cell lymphoma infusion products; those associations did not prove that one engineered modification would correct every failure.
records.principle: A common CAR presents a binder outside the cell and signaling domains inside it, connected through a spacer and transmembrane region. Conventional surface-antigen recognition can bypass peptide-HLA presentation; specialized peptide-HLA-targeting CARs retain the relevant HLA and antigen-processing requirements.
strengths: Antigen-directed recognition in engineered T cells
Established uses for specific products in selected blood cancers
limitations: Shared healthy-tissue targets and inflammatory, neurologic or blood-count harms
Manufacturing, access and cost depend on the product and setting
Antigen heterogeneity, cell state, tissue access and local inhibition

records.name: TCR-T cell therapy
records.tldr: TCR-T supplies living T cells carrying a selected receptor that recognizes a specified peptide with its presenting HLA molecule. A source-protein name alone does not establish that target.
records.summary:
Conventional alpha-beta TCR-T introduces selected paired receptor-chain instructions into therapeutic T cells. The receptor recognizes a displayed peptide-HLA complex, rather than entering the tumor cell to bind the whole source protein. Natural processing, the required HLA allele, surface display, receptor expression and useful cell function remain different questions. This differs from administering a soluble TCR/CD3 protein that recruits other T cells.

Afamitresgene autoleucel (Tecelra) is an approved TCR-T example. FDA initially approved it in 2024 and converted the specified adult use to traditional approval in June 2026, extending the indication to patients aged 12 and older. Its synovial-sarcoma indication retains prior-chemotherapy, selected HLA and MAGE-A4 testing requirements. The full label also contains exclusions and safety requirements; a broad HLA-A*02 label is not a complete eligibility rule.

notes: Morgan transferred receptor genes into autologous lymphocytes in a metastatic-melanoma study. Introducing selected recognition instructions differs from expanding a tumor-derived population with its existing receptors. Viral transduction describes a delivery method, not the definition of every receptor-engineering process.

The conventional receptor uses paired alpha and beta chains alongside the CD3 complex. Cloning selected receptor coding sequences means copying instructions; one sequenced chain does not establish a complete functional receptor or its specificity. Expression and assembly in the finished cells require evaluation. The Dong structural study distinguishes recognition chains from associated signaling components. Bendle showed in mouse models that introduced and endogenous chains could form self-reactive mixed receptors; vector and cell-population changes reduced that model risk. This does not supply a clinical risk rate for every TCR-T product.

Protein expression and HLA typing lie upstream of the displayed ligand. Antigen/HLA loss or impaired presentation can remove one recognition route; retaining another allele does not rescue a receptor requiring the lost allele. A different receptor using a retained allele needs its own specificity and functional evidence.

In research, test paired receptor expression and naturally presenting targets, with relevant antigen/HLA removal and restoration, irrelevant peptides, unmodified effectors and healthy tissue. Multimer or peptide-loaded reagent binding is different from natural processing, target-cell death or patient benefit. This research validation is distinct from the approved product’s clinical testing rule.

Cameron investigated fatal cardiac toxicity with one affinity-enhanced MAGE-A3 receptor and identified a cross-reactive Titin peptide presented by HLA-A*01 as the most likely cause. Earlier screening had not detected the hazard. This was a different receptor from the MAGE-A4 product Tecelra; stronger binding does not establish improved specificity or safety for either a new construct or an entire family.

The June 2026 Tecelra label names HLA-A*02:01P, -A*02:02P, -A*02:03P and -A*02:06P and a MAGE-A4 tumor test in its indication, with a separate HLA-A*02:05P contraindication. The approval letter documents the adult conversion and pediatric expansion. These are product-specific regulatory scopes, not a general rule for every TCR-T.

Conventional surface-antigen CARs and peptide-HLA-directed receptors have different recognition requirements, but peptide-HLA CARs also exist. The WT1/HLA-A*24:02 CAR study is a preclinical counterexample to saying all intracellular source antigens are unreachable by any CAR. A format change does not supply a missing required peptide-HLA complex.

For a soluble TCR/CD3 protein, the dosed molecule supplies recognition and recruits available T cells. TCR-T instead supplies receptor-bearing living cells. Protein exposure, cell trafficking/persistence and useful target-dependent function need separate measurements; neither format wins by definition.
records.principle: Selected alpha-beta recognition chains operate with the cell’s CD3 signaling machinery. The intended target is the particular naturally displayed peptide-HLA complex, not genotype, RNA abundance or source protein alone.
strengths: Can investigate targets derived from intracellular proteins through peptide-HLA display
A selected receptor can confer recognition on engineered cells in defined settings
limitations: Allele and antigen-processing/display dependencies can limit recognition
Cross-reactivity, healthy-tissue recognition and whole-regimen harms require evaluation
Receptor-positive cells still need appropriate state, tissue access and function

records.name: Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC)
records.tldr: An antibody-drug conjugate links a target-binding antibody to an active drug. Binding, delivery, release and drug action each matter, and normal tissues can also be exposed.
records.summary: The antibody recognizes an accessible antigen; the attachment chemistry and linker affect stability and release; the payload acts through its own molecular mechanism. Cytotoxic examples include TOP1 inhibitors, tubulin inhibitors and DNA-damaging agents. Uptake and lysosomal processing are important for many constructs, while some linkers also release drug outside cells. A surface antigen can be a delivery address without being a driver the tumor depends on. The dose, mean loading, loading distribution, released species and exposure must be interpreted for the finished product. There is no universal fold improvement in the therapeutic window.

notes: The treatment and diagnostic labels retain product-specific indications and testing requirements. A companion diagnostic validated for one drug or intended use is not automatically interchangeable with another. Keep the study population, comparator and prior exposure with any clinical result; a binding result or shared antigen name does not transfer benefit.

Follow the complete construct through separate measurements. Controlled binding to viable cells tests an accessible recognition feature; fixed-tissue staining alone does not. A trafficking assay must distinguish surface-bound from internal material. Measuring the relevant released payload or catabolite at its site of action tests a later step, and a payload-appropriate functional readout and survival over time answer further questions. A fluorescent antibody-associated tag can remain detectable without demonstrating that active drug reached that compartment. Keep assay sensitivity, time, concentration, cellular denominator and controls with each result; no one of these measurements establishes delivery throughout a tumour or clinical benefit.

In a fictional model, a tissue stain names protein M and controlled live-cell tests show antibody binding. Four proposed products still need different experiments: a blocking antibody needs a relevant signal and survival readout; a conjugate needs active-material delivery and a response to that material; an engager needs useful T cells, target-negative and no-T-cell controls, and completed target-cell killing; a radiolabelled product needs distribution over time and tumour and normal-organ dosimetry. The observed binding does not supply those unmeasured results. A model can also omit normal tissues, immune cells, spatial variation or clinically achievable exposure.

Choosing a surface address involves its measured amount, accessible normal-tissue distribution, behaviour with the actual format and variation within and between lesions. One positive core at one date cannot survey the whole tumour. A static receptor count and a manufactured loading ratio do not alone determine cumulative delivery across receptor turnover, repeated encounters and release over time. ADC uptake and processing are construct-specific; antibody retention can matter to radiation delivery, and engager contact geometry and useful effectors matter to immune recruitment. No universal antigen-density cutoff or low-density format ranking follows from a platform name. Damelin's 2015 survey found a broad range of normal- and tumour-tissue expression among the ADC targets studied and could not formalise optimal target parameters within that set. It does not show that useful target selection is impossible.

A change of format is a new product hypothesis. If an ADC binds M but yields little active material after uptake, an M-directed engager might avoid that particular processing requirement. It still needs its own binding and contact-geometry measurements, useful effector access and function, normal-tissue testing and clinical evidence. Earlier antibody or ADC tolerability does not establish the safety of a different action. Bystander delivery and two-address designs are possible responses to heterogeneous expression, not guaranteed coverage or an exhaustive list of solutions.

Compare requirements rather than rank formats. Trastuzumab can inhibit proliferation and recruit antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity; the related HER2 antibody in trastuzumab deruxtecan carries a TOP1-inhibitor payload. An ADC and a surface T-cell engager differ in processing versus productive contact with useful effectors. An engager recruits responders, whereas a CAR-T product supplies engineered living cells with their own survival, expansion and trafficking. A radioligand's carrier distribution and radiation deposition differ from chemical-payload delivery. Sharing an address does not equalise any of these actions, exposure histories or normal-tissue risks. With a clinical claim, record disease, biomarker definition, prior care, comparator, endpoint, follow-up and harms alongside the actual product; access or eligibility cannot supply an unmeasured efficacy comparison.

Four U.S. breast-cancer label examples separate address from payload: sacituzumab govitecan pairs TROP2 with SN-38, datopotamab deruxtecan pairs TROP2 with DXd, trastuzumab deruxtecan pairs HER2 with DXd, and trastuzumab emtansine pairs HER2 with DM1. SN-38 and DXd inhibit TOP1; DM1 acts on microtubules. Their indication and testing requirements differ, including the HER2-positive uses of T-DM1 and specified lower-expression uses of T-DXd. Changing the address or payload changes a design feature, not a measured probability of response. These examples are not an exhaustive U.S. or worldwide approval inventory.

Lymphoma: binding and antigen abundance do not by themselves establish usable payload delivery. Internalization, intracellular processing and payload transport need construct-specific evidence. CD20 is not universally non-internalizing: rituximab-CD20 uptake varied with target-cell Fc-gamma receptor IIb in the cited experiments. Lysosomal-transporter experiments with other conjugates also show that a block after uptake can cause resistance. These observations do not establish one limiting toxicity for all lymphoma ADCs.
records.principle: Binding can support delivery, but uptake, processing, access to the payload’s target and cellular response require separate evidence.
records.generation: Attachment chemistry, payload and delivery format vary across products
strengths: Can deliver an active drug through a selected molecular address
Some constructs kill neighboring target-negative cells in defined models
limitations: Normal-tissue exposure and product-specific lung, blood-cell, nerve or eye toxicity remain possible
Antigen, trafficking, release, efflux and cell-response changes can cause resistance
Binding or an expression score alone does not establish benefit

records.name: T-cell engagers (bispecific)
records.tldr: T-cell engagers are proteins that bind a specified target and recruit T cells, often through CD3. A binding bridge does not by itself establish completed killing.
records.summary:
A dosed T-cell engager supplies a protein connecting target recognition to an available T cell. It does not itself install receptor instructions or supply engineered living responders. Product design can use antibody-derived binding fragments or a soluble TCR recognition domain; some target arms require a particular peptide-HLA complex. Compact BiTE designs, Fc-containing architectures and half-life extension describe features that can overlap rather than mutually exclusive treatment categories.

Clinical examples include blinatumomab in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, teclistamab in multiple myeloma and tarlatamab in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Their actual labels define different settings, combinations, prior treatments and harms. Tebentafusp is a peptide-HLA-directed soluble TCR/CD3 protein with its own allele- and disease-specific use. Neither a common platform name nor binding in a laboratory establishes eligibility or comparative benefit.

notes: An antibody-derived TCR mimic recognizes a peptide-HLA complex using an antibody scaffold. A soluble TCR/CD3 engager instead uses a TCR-derived recognition scaffold attached to a recruiting arm. TCR-T administers cells carrying receptor chains. Target recognition, molecular scaffold and administered object are separate axes; a mimic can be part of an engager without becoming a TCR protein.

Liddy studied soluble TCR/CD3 ImmTAC proteins in experimental systems. Dao studied an antibody-derived WT1/HLA-A*02:01/CD3 engager in cells and mice. Their results do not establish clinical benefit for every scaffold, HLA allele or cancer. Recruiting another T cell does not require that cell’s native receptor to recognize the target, but does not remove the target arm’s HLA restriction.

The KIMMTRAK label identifies tebentafusp as a soluble gp100 peptide-HLA/CD3 protein for HLA-A*02:01-positive adults with unresectable or metastatic uveal melanoma. This is a named clinical protein example, not an engineered-cell product or evidence that other peptide-HLA binders share its indication or outcomes.

Binding to supplied peptide-HLA reagent can bypass natural processing and display. Source-protein expression or a compatible genotype alone is not a functional target assay. For a research claim, compare naturally presenting targets, irrelevant peptides, the wrong HLA allele, antigen-negative targets, suitable effector cells, no-effector conditions and healthy tissues. Labeled clinical selection tests remain a separate clinical-use rule. Record the peptide sequence, HLA allele, display method and its detection or recovery limits; no universal target-density cutoff follows from the format name.

The Mack construct joined two single-chain Fv fragments with a peptide linker in one compact protein; this is different from an IgG architecture with an Fc region. The FDA tarlatamab application describes DLL3/CD3 binding domains combined with an IgG Fc region in a half-life-extended BiTE. Thus BiTE, Fc-containing and half-life-extended are not three exclusive buckets. Fc design, binding geometry, affinity, target density, distribution and measured exposure still belong to the specific molecule. The Giffin cell, mouse and nonhuman-primate study does not define a universal human schedule.

Compare recognition, T-cell activation, proliferation, target death, cytokine release and protein exposure at named times. Record effector source/state, target density, effector-to-target ratio, dose or concentration and denominator; include target-negative and no-effector controls. A granule or cytokine signal does not substitute for completed target-cell death or clinical benefit. Cytokines in a culture are a measured laboratory endpoint, not a diagnosis of clinical cytokine-release syndrome.

Bluemel compared epitope positions and antigen sizes in engineered cell systems. Constructs with similar target-binding affinity differed in target-cell lysis, supporting functional testing of the actual geometry rather than ranking every molecule by affinity alone. In the solitomab phase 1 solid-tumor study, dose-limiting diarrhea and liver abnormalities constrained dose escalation; an accessible target and a binding bridge did not by themselves establish a useful therapeutic window.

Compared with administered CAR-T or TCR-T cells, a protein engager recruits effectors rather than supplying engineered responders. Protein mass/concentration and viable-cell dose have different units; clearance differs from cell survival, expansion and trafficking. A shared target name does not establish matched epitope, affinity, contact geometry, exposure, controllability or safety.

The 2025 FDA tarlatamab decision followed the randomized DeLLphi-304 comparison after platinum-based treatment in SCLC. Its survival finding belongs to that drug and setting. The cited blinatumomab consolidation and teclistamab combination/monotherapy decisions likewise retain their own settings; none is a class-wide treatment-sequencing rule.

Stopping a protein infusion and reversing an injury are different outcomes. In Kebenko's 2018 phase 1 solitomab study of 65 patients with refractory solid tumours, the reported half-life was 4.5 hours. Diarrhoea limited dosing; one grade 3 event progressed to grade 5 after solitomab discontinuation. That observation shows why short measured protein exposure does not guarantee immediate reversal of toxicity. It is one product and study, not a rate or a safety rule for all engagers. Living engineered cells have their own expansion, persistence and trafficking, rather than sharing this protein's clearance clock.

For a lymphoma engager, target presence, access to suitable T cells and useful effector function need separate evidence. Antigen expression alone does not establish these other steps. These biological questions do not by themselves select an earlier treatment line; treatment timing needs evidence for the actual drug and setting.
records.principle: A specified target-binding region and T-cell-recruiting region promote encounters. CD3 recruitment can bypass the recruited cell’s own antigen specificity; a peptide-HLA-binding target arm still retains its peptide and HLA requirements.
strengths: Established clinical uses for particular products in defined settings
Protein exposure can be adjusted through a specified dosing regimen
limitations: Productive encounters need accessible targets and functional effectors
Healthy-tissue recognition, cytokine release and neurologic harms need product-specific evidence
Stopping administration does not instantly clear protein or reverse an effect already triggered

records.name: Radio-antibody & radio-ADC
records.tldr: Radioimmunotherapy uses an antibody or antibody fragment to carry a radionuclide. Its radiation delivery and safety depend on the complete labeled product.
records.summary: An antibody provides recognition while the radionuclide provides radiation. This differs from releasing a small-molecule cytotoxic drug after intracellular processing. Attachment chemistry depends on the isotope and product; a chelator is not required for every radionuclide. In a historical phase 2 study, lutetium-177-J591 targeted PSMA in men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and produced substantial hematologic toxicity. That disease-specific experience does not establish current approval, breast-cancer efficacy or the suitability of every ADC antigen for radioimmunotherapy.

notes: Crossfire means radiation from one location reaching nearby cells. It is distinct from a diffusible chemical payload and does not require the same release chemistry. Neither crossfire nor an immune-effect hypothesis establishes clinical benefit after ADC resistance.
records.principle: The labeled antibody’s distribution and retention, radionuclide emissions and tissue geometry determine where radiation is deposited.
strengths: Can deliver radiation with an antibody recognition route
Particles can reach cells beyond the bound target cell
limitations: Circulating and normal-organ radioactivity can cause toxicity
Target expression alone does not establish sufficient tumor dose
Antibody and small-ligand kinetics are not interchangeable
